finding.claim: SSRF: the iconUrl supplied to PUT /profile is stored with no validation and is fetched server-side by the nightly sync job. An attacker can point it at internal services, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) or localhost. The response body is read as bytes, so it may be exposed or stored. Even a blind GET against internal endpoints is a risk. Ledger: E1 PUT /profile (webhook, icon), E2 nightly job (second-order). S1 HttpClient.send on webhookUrl (line 21) is SAFE because the regex is anchored by String.matches, which requires a full match, against a fixed host. S2 HttpClient.send on iconUrl (line 23) is VULNERABLE.
finding.source: The `icon` parameter of Profile.update (PUT /profile), line 11, stored in this.iconUrl at line 16

trace.note: this.iconUrl = icon, stored with no scheme, host, or IP validation (only webhook is checked, at line 12)
sync() later calls URI.create(iconUrl) and issues a GET from the server

finding.guards_checked: The regex check at line 12 applies only to `webhook`, not to `icon`. There is no allowlist, scheme check, private or link-local IP blocking, or DNS pinning on iconUrl. The HttpClient `c` is injected and its redirect policy is not visible here (the Java default is NEVER). No guard on the iconUrl path was found.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores the attacker-supplied `icon` unvalidated (the only check, at line 12, covers `webhook`), and src/Profile.java:23 fetches it server-side with HttpClient.send, so there is no closing guard.
